title: Variance and EV
summary: Why correct play can lose, and how to judge decisions.

idea.text:
**Variance** is how results scatter around what is expected. In poker luck decides a single hand and even a session, but in the long run the player with better **EV** (expected value) decisions wins.

Example: AA against KK before the flop wins about **82%** of the time. So in roughly one hand out of five the aces lose, and that is normal, not "unfair".

judge.text:
How to judge your play:
- Judge **decisions**, not results. A good call can lose and a bad one can win.
- Look at **all-in EV**: how much you should have won by the odds when the chips went in. The hand analysis shows it.
- Draw conclusions from a **large sample**: hundreds and thousands of hands, not one evening.

labels: The kings got there: it happens about 18% of the time

q-ev.q: You called an all-in with 60% equity and lost. How do you rate the call?
options: Correct: it wins chips in the long run
q-ev.explain: A decision with 60% equity where 50% was needed is profitable even if this hand was lost.

options: Results scattering around what is expected
t1.explain: Variance is the swing in results caused by the luck of the cards.

t2.q: What is the best way to judge your play?
options: Decision quality over a large sample
t2.explain: Short-term results say almost nothing about the quality of play.

t3.q: AA against KK before the flop. How often do the kings win?
t3.explain: The aces win about 82%, the kings about 18%.
